title: Prefix Suggestions
statement: A search box suggests catalog words while a visitor types. Given distinct lowercase words and the full text typed, return a list with one entry per typed character: after typing the first i characters, the entry holds up to three catalog words that start with those characters, in alphabetical order (the three smallest). When nothing matches, the entry is an empty list.
constraints: words are distinct and contain only a-z; typed contains only a-z

examples.explanation: After 'm' the three smallest matches are mango, map, mast; after 'ma' they are the same; after 'mas' only mast remains.
'k' and 'ki' match both words; 'kix' matches nothing.

hints.content: Each keystroke only extends the previous prefix by one character, so the matching words can only shrink.
In a trie (prefix tree), every word is a path from the root, and all words sharing a prefix pass through that prefix's node.
If each node remembered its best suggestions, answering a keystroke would be a single step down the tree.
Insert the words in alphabetical order. Then each node only needs to keep the first three words that pass through it.
Walk the typed letters from the root, reading each node's saved list. Once a letter has no child, every later prefix has no matches either.

testCases.explanation: After 'm' the three smallest matches are mango, map, mast; after 'ma' they are the same; after 'mas' only mast remains.
'k' and 'ki' match both words; 'kix' matches nothing.
The word itself is suggested at every step.
A word that equals the prefix counts as a match.
Only the three smallest are kept, and the last step matches nothing.
Five matches are trimmed to three.

solutions.title: Filter and sort for every prefix
solutions.intuition: Directly apply the definition: for each prefix, collect the words that start with it.
solutions.approach: For each length from 1 to typed.length, filter words by startsWith, sort them, and keep the first three.
solutions.pseudocode:
for i in 1..len(typed): p = typed[0:i]; out.push(sorted(w for w in words if w startsWith p)[0:3])
return out
solutions.timeComplexity: O(m · n log n · L) for m typed characters, n words of length up to L
solutions.interviewExplanation: This applies the definition directly. It re-filters and re-sorts the whole catalog for every keystroke, so it does far more work than needed.

steps.title: Step 1
steps.content: For typed 'mas', prefix 'm' matches all five words; sorted: mango, map, mast, mat, melon. Keep three.

solutions.title: Trie with the three best words at each node
solutions.intuition: All words sharing a prefix pass through one trie node, so the node can remember that prefix's three smallest words ahead of time.
solutions.approach: Sort the words and insert them into a trie in that order. Along each word's path, append the word to a node's list if it holds fewer than three. Then walk the typed letters from the root, outputting each node's list, or an empty list once the path falls off the trie.
solutions.pseudocode:
root = node(); for w in sorted(words): n = root; for ch in w: n = n.child(ch) or create; if len(n.top) < 3: n.top.push(w)
n = root; for ch in typed: n = n and n.child(ch); out.push(n ? n.top : [])
solutions.timeComplexity: O(n log n · L) to build, then O(1) per keystroke
commonMistakes: Inserting words unsorted and keeping the first three, which keeps arbitrary words instead of the smallest.
Continuing to read children after the path has fallen off the trie, which throws on undefined.
solutions.interviewExplanation: I build a trie from the words in sorted order, and each node stores the first three words that pass through it, which are its prefix's three smallest matches. Each keystroke then moves one step down the tree and reads the saved list. Once a letter has no child, every later prefix is empty too. Building costs a sort plus the total length of the words, and queries are O(1) each. The trade-off is memory for the nodes. Sorting with binary search is a lighter alternative.

steps.title: Step 1
steps.content: Sorted words: mango, map, mast, mat, melon. Node 'm' keeps mango, map, mast. Node 'ma' keeps the same three.

steps.title: Step 2
steps.content: Node 'mas' is reached only by mast, so it keeps [mast].

steps.title: Step 3
steps.content: Typing 'mas' reads [mango, map, mast], [mango, map, mast], [mast].

solutions.title: Sort once and binary search each prefix
solutions.intuition: Sorted order groups each prefix's matches into one block, and the block for a longer prefix sits inside the block for a shorter one.
solutions.approach: Sort the words once. For each prefix, binary search the first index whose word is >= prefix, starting no earlier than the previous answer. Read up to three words from there while they start with the prefix.
solutions.pseudocode:
sort words; low = 0
for each prefix p: lo = lower_bound(words, p, from low); low = lo
  take up to 3 words from lo while they start with p
solutions.timeComplexity: O(n log n · L + m · (log n + L))
commonMistakes: Sorting the caller's array in place.
Forgetting that the lower bound for a longer prefix can only be at or after the previous one; resetting is correct but slower, moving backward is a bug.
solutions.interviewExplanation: I sort once so every prefix's matches form a contiguous block. For each keystroke I binary search for the first word that's at least the prefix, then read at most three words while they still match. Prefixes only grow, so the lower bound is monotone and I can reuse it. Sorting dominates. Compared with the trie it uses less memory, but each keystroke costs a binary search instead of one step.

steps.title: Step 1
steps.content: Sorted: mango, map, mast, mat, melon.

steps.title: Step 2
steps.content: Prefix 'm' starts at index 0: mango, map, mast. Prefix 'ma' also starts at 0.

steps.title: Step 3
steps.content: Prefix 'mas' starts at index 2 (mast); mat does not start with 'mas', so only mast is suggested.
